3.text: von Maydell, the natives pointed out to me that at present the families who

4.text: in Maydell’s time were dependent on other people’s herds, had for their

5.text: subsistence, as a rule, herds of their own. On the Omolon, Eiˊheli, the son

6.text: of Amraˊkwurg̣ɪn, — the rich herdsman (now deceased) who was selected by

7.text: Maydell for the position of “principal chief,” — had five large herds instead

8.text: of the two of his father.¹ His brother-in-law and one of his cousins had three

9.text: each, etc. In 1901, however, I heard in Anadyr that the reindeer-herds in the

10.text: Omolon country were greatly reduced by the hoof-disease.

11.text: I mentioned before that the inhabitants of several maritime villages have

12.text: turned reindeer-breeders, and that even some of the Asiatic Eskimo have acquired

13.text: reindeer-herds. Thus Kuvaˊr of Indian Point had two large herds that he had

14.text: placed in charge of a Reindeer-Chukchee friend, whom he kept supplied with

15.text: every American, Russian, or Eskimo ware required for the use of his family.

16.text: DOMESTICATED REINDEER. — There are several races of domesticated rein-

17.text: deer. The Chukchee reindeer (tɪmñêˊ-qor, “ordinary reindeer”) is distinctively

18.text: different from the Lamut reindeer (waˊwa-qor or waˊwaq). It is undersized,

19.text: its legs are shorter, body heavier, head not so long, the antlers thicker and

20.text: heavier and the difference between buck and doe in this respect less marked,

21.text: and the general color of the animal of darker hue. The Koryak reindeer is

22.text: still smaller and darker than that of the Chukchee. The Lamut reindeer on

23.text: the Sea of Okhotsk is large, and the darkest of all. The Chukchee reindeer

24.text: is quite unfit for the saddle, and is not so strong in the harness, especially

25.text: in heavy snow, as the Lamut reindeer; but it is much better for slaughter,

26.text: since it fattens quickly, and does not lose its fat as easily. In good pasture

27.text: the Chukchee reindeer accumulates so much fat that its whole body is covered

28.text: with it. On the hind part, near the tail, the fat is about two inches thick.

29.text: At present a brisk trade in reindeer is carried on between the Lamut

30.text: and the Chukchee. The Lamut reindeer commands about twice the price of

31.text: the Chukchee reindeer. Usually a Lamut fawn is exchanged for a grown

32.text: Chukchee reindeer. A broken Lamut reindeer is worth three Chukchee rein-

33.text: deer; and the Lamut and the Tungus often break all the young bucks in

34.text: their herds in order to barter them away to the Chukchee. Therefore the

35.text: larger portion of Chukchee harness-reindeer are at the present time of the

36.text: Lamut race. The Lamut, on the other hand, have stopped slaughtering their

37.text: own reindeer, because they can always get Chukchee reindeer, which are

38.text: cheaper, and better fitted for the purpose.

39.text: Crossing between tame and wild reindeer frequently occurs, especially in

40.text: the Chukchee herds, although with the wild reindeer the rutting-season begins

41.text: a couple of weeks later than with the tame one. One by one wild bucks
